references.text: The woman had just expressed her expectation of the Messiah in John 4:25, and now in verse 29 she asks whether Jesus can be the Christ, based on his telling her everything she had done.

In John 4:17–19, Jesus revealed details about the woman’s life—that she had had five husbands and that the man she currently had was not her husband. This is the background for her words, "He told me all that I have done".
In John 4:39 we see the result of the woman’s testimony: many Samaritans came to believe in Jesus precisely because of her words, "He told me all that I have done".
In John 1:41 Andrew finds his brother Simon and says, "We have found the Messiah". The woman’s question in 4:29 is a parallel invitation for others to come and see whether Jesus is the Christ.
In John 1:45–46 Philip invites Nathanael with the words, "Come and see!"—the same fundamental testimony that the woman gives: "Come and see a man…".

In John 7:26 the crowd asks a similar question: "Could it be that the rulers have really recognized that he is the Messiah?" The question form with μήτι expresses cautious wonder, in the same way as the woman’s question in 4:29.
John 2:25 says that Jesus knew what was in man and did not need anyone to testify about man. The woman’s experience of Jesus telling her everything she had done confirms this supernatural knowledge.

In Deuteronomy 18:15 it is promised that the Lord will raise up a prophet. The Samaritans were waiting for this figure (Taheb), and the woman’s question about whether Jesus is the Christ can be linked to this expectation.
In John 4:42 the Samaritans themselves confirm that Jesus is "the Savior of the world", and thus the woman’s question from verse 29 is answered affirmatively—he truly is the Christ.
In John 16:30 the disciples say, "Now we know that you know all things". This reflects the woman’s experience: Jesus knew everything she had done, which pointed to his divine identity.
